## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

_Why does a capable model still need a precise contract around every call?_

A model call can return a response that parses cleanly yet violates the tool schema, arrives past its deadline, or claims a file edit succeeded before any tool has run. Because every capability an agent adds—tool dispatch, memory retrieval, sandboxed execution, and recovery—is built from individual model calls, any ambiguity at the call boundary spreads into every subsystem downstream. A foundation model is an ungrounded token predictor that emits candidate proposals across an untrusted boundary, not a verified state transition. The surrounding runtime must therefore enforce reliability at each call through token budgets, schema checks, and independent verification. Within the H·S·A exposure space, the single call sits at the origin: one bounded turn, zero carried state, and zero ambient authority.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Explain the separate responsibilities of the foundation model, inference service, and agent runtime
- Construct a token-bounded request containing task messages, advertised tools, and generation limits
- Calculate how temperature and nucleus truncation reshape candidates without establishing correctness, and explain why only a recorded call replays exactly
- Diagnose response outcomes using completion status, structural validity, permission checks, and external evidence that self-review cannot supply
- Distinguish the guarantees of grammar-constrained decoding from learned formatting and correct task values
- Estimate call latency and repeated-input work under explicit serving and prefix-reuse assumptions
- Evaluate interface representations using accepted outcomes and resource use under matched task budgets

:::

## One Turn of the Repair Loop {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-introduction}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_origin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with all three axes gray and only the origin dot highlighted in purple."}

*A single call runs one turn, carries no state, and holds zero ambient authority.*
:::

The repair agent (@sec-vol3-intro-lighthouses) needs to inspect the connection-pool implementation before proposing a change. A model call that emits `read_file("src/pool.py")` produces only an unexecuted text string. Of the six phases of a turn (@sec-vol3-intro-execution-lifecycle), only the call itself belongs to the model; checking the path, authorizing the read, running it, and returning the observation all belong to the runtime. This loop of model-generated proposals and runtime observations is the interaction pattern formalized by ReAct [@yao2023react], and every runtime phase depends on knowing what the single model phase delivers.

In a chat window, a human reader spots a response cut off mid-sentence, judges whether a shell command is safe to run, and waits out variable generation delays. An autonomous agent removes that human reader. The runtime receives the response as data and must check in code what a person would judge by eye: whether the prompt fit inside the context window, whether generation finished normally or hit the output token limit, whether a well-formed tool request targets a path inside the allowed workspace, and how much time and budget the call spent. Raw reply text cannot answer those questions; a runtime that guesses call state by scraping output strings will eventually apply a truncated patch or run a command outside its workspace.

Preventing those failures requires an explicit call contract between the agent runtime and the inference service. That contract covers both directions of the call: the outbound request (message history, advertised tool definitions, and token and time limits) and the inbound response record (payload kind, stop reason, normalized status, and token usage). It also fixes the checks the runtime runs before dispatching any proposed action, along with the latency and input-recomputation costs of each call. Rather than assuming the model is reliable, the contract treats the inference service as an untrusted, probabilistic generator and keeps every control-flow decision in the runtime.

The chapter follows the repair agent's single inspection call from request to bill, adding one runtime obligation at each step. Before the call is sent, the runtime must know who owns which decision (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-role) and whether the serialized request fits with room left for an answer (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-tokenization). How the service then produces a candidate (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-autoregressive) explains why repeated calls differ and why generation can stop before the candidate is whole. That possibility fixes the order of the checks on the way back. The runtime first reads the call's normalized status to learn whether a complete candidate arrived at all (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract), then asks which property each check on a completed candidate actually establishes (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-continuations), and finally whether syntax errors can be prevented during generation instead of rejected after it (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-grammar-constrained). The last two sections price the call. Output length and re-sent history set its latency and work (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost), and those costs decide how competing output representations should be compared, on accepted repairs under a matched budget (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-interface-design).

## The Model Call Boundary {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-role}

If a runtime treats a model's output string `read_file("src/pool.py")` as an already-authorized file read, a single hallucinated path can read outside the workspace before any check runs. Keeping a proposed action separate from an executed one requires splitting each call across three components: the foundation model, the inference service, and the agent runtime. The foundation model[^fn-foundation-model-term] computes conditional probability distributions over token sequences given a prompt context. The **inference service**\index{Inference service!definition} hosts the model weights, runs forward passes on accelerators, applies sampling parameters, and packages the output tokens into a response record. The agent runtime drives the task: it builds the prompt, tracks budgets, checks candidate outputs, and decides whether an action is allowed to run in the host environment. Even when all three run in the same process on one machine, their interfaces keep generated text separate from the decision to act on it.

[^fn-foundation-model-term]: **Homogenization**: The same report that named foundation models warned that, because many applications adapt one shared base model, a defect in that model passes into every system built on it [@bommasani2021opportunities]. For autonomous agents the warning is concrete. Every runtime that invokes the same model and serving path inherits the same failure modes at once, so the runtime, rather than the model, must hold the operational checks. \index{Foundation model!homogenization}

::: {#dfn-vol3-proposal .callout-definition title="Proposal"}

A ***proposal***\index{Proposal!definition} is model output that specifies a candidate action or answer for the runtime to evaluate, carrying zero ambient authority and producing no external side effects until the runtime explicitly validates, authorizes, and executes it.

1.  **Significance**: Every external effect of an agent depends on an explicit runtime decision. Because the model call possesses zero ambient authority, a rejected proposal costs one inference invocation rather than an unintended modification to the environment. That invocation still consumes resources and counts toward $\AttemptCost$ in the cost per accepted task (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task).
2.  **Distinction**: A proposal must not be confused with an *effect* (a state change executed by the runtime after authorization) or an *observation* (the runtime's factual record of what an operation returned). Emitting `read_file("src/pool.py")` is merely a proposal; the file contents subsequently retrieved from disk and supplied to the next call constitute an observation.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Logging a tool request as an executed action, or accepting a model's textual claim that "the file has been read" as an empirical observation, allows fluent prose to stand in for operational evidence.

:::

### Messages and tool definitions {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-messages-tool-definitions}

A model cannot tell an operator's instruction, a user's prompt, and a file excerpt returned by a tool apart unless the runtime labels each piece of the request, yet those labels alone do not make the content trustworthy. The runtime organizes the prompt as an ordered sequence of role-tagged messages\index{Model invocation contract!messages and roles}: a `system` message sets task instructions and constraints, a `user` message supplies the task prompt, an `assistant` message records earlier model outputs, and a `tool` message carries the raw observation returned when an action runs. Role tags organize the token stream for the model's attention mechanism, while the runtime remains responsible for checking whether the content is authentic and follows the task contract.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The task contract, which fixes the goal, environment, permitted actions, available observations, and completion criteria, is established in @sec-vol3-intro-five-part-contract.
:::

Alongside the message history, the request advertises the tools available to the model and gives their argument schemas. In @lst-vol3-model-request, the runtime declares a file-reading tool with one required string parameter. The JSON-schema definition tells the model what syntax a valid proposal needs, while the runtime enforces workspace sandboxing and filesystem permissions independently.

::: {#lst-vol3-model-request lst-cap="**A bounded inspection request**: This provider-neutral record separates model-visible messages and tool definitions from the configuration and limits governing the call. Symbolic values stand for settings chosen by the runtime; the field names do not prescribe a vendor API."}
```yaml
model_config: repair-model/config-a
messages:
  - role: system
    content: Propose the next inspection for the assigned repair.
  - role: user
    content: Inspect the connection-pool locking logic in src/pool.py.
tools:
  - name: read_file
    arguments_schema:
      type: object
      properties: {path: {type: string}}
      required: [path]
      additionalProperties: false
limits:
  max_output_tokens: K_max
  deadline: T_deadline
sampling: selected_sampling_settings
```
:::

The `model_config` field binds the request to a specific model version, weights checkpoint, and serving profile, while `sampling` controls how the service draws output tokens from the model's predicted distribution. Two resource bounds protect the call from running away: `max_output_tokens` ($\OutputLimit$) caps how many tokens the call can generate, and `deadline` ($\CompletionDeadline$) sets a timeout against queue delays and serving stalls. Writing those bounds into the request works only when the inference service or client runtime enforces them during generation.

When generation finishes, the inference service returns free-form text, a tool proposal, or a service error, and a runtime adapter normalizes that provider-specific reply into a single envelope (@lst-vol3-model-response). Here, the service reports a completed generation pass that produced a tool request to read `src/pool.py`—one diagnostic step before any repair is checked.

::: {#lst-vol3-model-response lst-cap="**A returned tool proposal**: Response kind identifies what the payload represents, while status and stop reason describe the invocation. Usage counts describe consumed generation resources, not progress on the repair."}
```yaml
kind: tool_request
payload:
  name: read_file
  arguments: {path: src/pool.py}
stop_reason: tool_request
status: COMPLETED
usage: {input_tokens: S, output_tokens: K}
```
:::

Here, `kind` tells the runtime parser how to read the payload. The normalized `status` confirms that transport and generation finished under the adapter's contract, while `stop_reason` records the **stop reason**\index{Stop reason!definition} reported by the serving engine: whether the model emitted a tool-call marker, hit an end-of-sequence token, or stopped at the token limit. The `usage` block counts $\SequenceLength$ input tokens read and $\OutputLength$ output tokens generated. Bare $\SequenceLength$ is sequence length throughout this book, here the prompt a call reads; the State levels $\Glyph{S}_0$ to $\Glyph{S}_3$ always carry their subscript. Tracking usage across calls prevents context-window overflow and feeds cost accounting; if a provider omits token counts, the runtime records usage as missing rather than zero.

Every path out of the response ends in the runtime, and the stop reason chooses the path (@fig-vol3-model-call-surface). A tool call goes to validation and authorization before anything runs, a finished answer goes to verification, and output cut off at its limit goes to quarantine, where it is kept for diagnosis and never executed (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-status-envelope states the rule).

::: {#fig-vol3-model-call-surface fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Model Call Surface**: The request carries messages, tool definitions, and limits into a model with frozen weights, which returns a proposal with a stop reason and usage counts. Every arrow out of the response lands in the agent runtime. The runtime validates and authorizes a tool call before anything runs, returns the result as a new message for the next call, sends a finished answer to verification, and quarantines output cut off at its limit." fig-alt="Diagram. A request card lists tools and limits above a stack of message slabs labeled system, user, assistant, and tool, the tool slab dashed. An arrow leads to a model box showing tokens y1, y2, y3 drawn one per step with frozen weights, and an arrow leads to a response card with rows for text, tool calls, usage, and a highlighted stop reason row. From the stop reason an arrow drops into an agent runtime region to a route on stop reason box. Its tool call branch goes to validate, authorize, then run in sandbox, and from the sandbox an arrow returns up to the tool slab of the request. Its end of turn branch goes to verify, and its output limit branch goes to a red quarantine box."}
![](images/svg/model_call_surface.svg)
:::

### Proposals and observations {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-proposals-observations}

If the runtime ran a returned `read_file` proposal directly against the host filesystem, a path like `../../etc/passwd` or a malformed argument would execute before any check caught it. Instead, the runtime passes every tool proposal through validation and authorization before anything runs. First, it checks structural conformance, confirming that the proposed arguments match the declared schema (for example, that `path` is a string rather than a shell command). Next, it checks the arguments against the task's permission grant: advertising `read_file` lets the model propose file reads, but grants no right to read arbitrary paths. The runtime verifies that `src/pool.py` resolves inside the allowed workspace rather than escaping to host files through directory traversal. Once authorized, the tool runs outside the model call, inside an isolated sandbox or container with its own timeout.

After the tool finishes, the runtime records what happened and builds the next prompt. It appends the model's `assistant` proposal paired with a `tool` message carrying the observation (here, the bounded file excerpt). That observation reports the actual outcome, including a missing file or a permission denial, and notes when the output was truncated; @sec-vol3-tool-calling-round-trip develops how the runtime matches each result to the call it answers, records errors, and marks truncation.

The model on the next turn sees the tool output only because the runtime rebuilds and sends the updated context window. Foundation models are stateless token predictors with no internal memory of earlier requests or tool runs. Session identifiers or server-side prefix caching (reusing attention state the service already computed for a prompt prefix that repeats across turns, priced in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-trajectory-cost-accumulation) can cut latency, but the runtime alone decides which messages enter the prompt. That separation also means an observation can go stale: a file excerpt in the prompt shows the file only as it stood when read, so if a later command edits the file on disk, the excerpt in context is out of date.

The gap between a proposal and an observation is where the fail-plausible fault enters. A model can emit a well-formed proposal targeting the wrong source module, or a convincing analysis grounded in an obsolete observation, and the tokens look the same either way. Agent engineering therefore requires treating status, schema structure, security authorization, and empirical evidence as distinct, non-fungible properties of the interaction. @Tbl-vol3-foundation-model-responsibilities summarizes what the runtime owns around every call, whether the model runs in the local process or behind a remote API.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The fail-plausible fault, output that looks well formed and credible while the intended property fails, is established in @sec-vol3-intro-fail-plausible.
:::

| Model term                  | Runtime responsibility                                                       | Failure if the runtime ignores it                                     |
|:----------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Context window**          | Count the complete input representation and reserve output headroom          | Rejected request or insufficient room for a complete response         |
| **Sampling settings**       | Choose supported settings and retain them with the request and output        | Unexplained variation or an unjustified assumption of reproducibility |
| **Tool call**               | Check the proposal, authorize access, and return the actual tool observation | A proposed operation mistaken for an executed or permitted one        |
| **Stop reason**             | Interpret it with normalized status before treating the payload as complete  | An interrupted or refused response treated as a finished candidate    |
| **Fluent but wrong output** | Evaluate the relevant claim using checks and observations with stated limits | Credibility mistaken for evidence of the intended property            |
| **Successful response**     | Distinguish delivery and generation completion from task acceptance          | A completed call recorded as a successful repair                      |
: **What the runtime owns around a model call**: Each feature of the call creates an obligation outside the model's generated content. Satisfying one obligation does not discharge the others. {#tbl-vol3-foundation-model-responsibilities}

The request and response records fix the boundary around a model call: messages supply context, tool definitions specify what the model may propose, and the runtime mediates every effect on external state. Before the service can run the call, however, the whole request must fit inside the model's context window with room left for the response, and checking that fit requires counting tokens rather than characters, messages, or files.

## Tokenizing the Request {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-tokenization}

When an automated repair agent appends a connection-pool source file and a compiler diagnostic to its message history, the payload expands rapidly. Naive metrics like file counts or raw character counts cannot determine whether the next request will fit within the model's capacity. Role delimiters, tool schemas, system prompts, file paths, and source code all serialize into a single sequence of discrete units before entering the neural network. The operational budget is the token count of that fully assembled sequence, measured strictly against the model's specific tokenizer and wire format.

### Tokens in the serialized request {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-serialized-request-tokens}

Estimating prompt size from character counts or source-code lexers fails because a model's **tokenizer**\index{Tokenizer!definition}\index{Tokenization|see{Tokenizer}} slices text into vocabulary identifiers whose boundaries rarely match words, identifiers, or JSON fields. Subword methods represent common fragments compactly while splitting unfamiliar words and identifiers into smaller pieces [@sennrich2016subword]. **Byte-pair encoding** (BPE)\index{Byte-pair encoding!definition}[^fn-bpe-compression-origin] learns repeated combinations of smaller units; other tokenizers use different segmentation rules, and some learn them directly from raw text without assuming word boundaries [@kudo2018sentencepiece]. Because a single token may represent a word, part of a word, whitespace, punctuation, or a combination of these, small formatting changes alter the token sequence.

[^fn-bpe-compression-origin]: **Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)**: The algorithm began as a data-compression scheme that repeatedly replaces the most frequent pair of adjacent bytes with an unused symbol [@gage1994bpe]; @sennrich2016subword repurposed the same merge rule to build open vocabularies for neural translation. Because the merges are learned from the training corpus's frequencies, the token cost of a string reflects how common it was in that corpus, so an unusual identifier or path can split into more tokens than a common word of the same length, and the runtime must count rather than estimate. \index{Byte-pair encoding!compression origin}

Indentation alone alters the resulting sequence. Under one widely used byte-pair vocabulary, `cl100k_base`, for example, the unindented line `def get_user_id():` encodes as five tokens beginning with `def` (identifier 755). Indenting that exact line by four spaces yields six tokens: three leading spaces (262), followed by ` def` with the fourth space fused to the keyword (711), and finally the remaining four tokens. A compiler lexer records indentation as block structure and emits the same keyword token at both levels; the model instead receives a different opening sequence of integer identifiers, with only the four tokens after the keyword shared (@fig-vol3-token-ast-mismatch).

::: {#fig-vol3-token-ast-mismatch fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**One Keyword, Two Token Sequences**: The same Python line, unindented and indented by four spaces, drawn on one character grid, with a compiler lexer's tokens above the characters and a byte-pair tokenizer's tokens below. The lexer records indentation as block structure and emits the same keyword and identifier for both lines. The tokenizer absorbs the fourth space into the keyword, so the indented line opens with two tokens that do not appear in the unindented one; only the four tokens after the keyword are shared. Identifiers are from the `cl100k_base` vocabulary." fig-alt="Two stacked blocks, unindented and indented by four spaces. Each block shows a row of character cells for the line def get_user_id():, with lexer tokens above and byte-pair tokens below, each token spanning the characters it covers. Lexer tokens are def, get_user_id, open parenthesis, close parenthesis, and colon; the indented line adds a dashed indent token over the four spaces. Byte-pair tokens for the unindented line are def 755, space get 636, _user 3398, _id 851, and parentheses colon 4658, labeled 5 tokens. For the indented line they are three spaces 262, space def 711, and the same four tokens, labeled 6 tokens. Tokens 755, 262, and 711 are filled dark; a dashed line marks where the lexer splits the indent from def, which the 711 token straddles. Brackets below mark the two leading tokens, where the fourth space joins the keyword, and the four tokens shared by both lines."}
![](images/svg/token_ast_mismatch.svg)
:::

In an inspection request, the string `src/pool.py` is a single path argument at the tool interface, yet it splits into several subword tokens at the model interface. Changing a file path, adding indentation, or escaping source code inside JSON shifts token boundaries in ways a fixed character-to-token ratio cannot predict. Neither JSON framing nor punctuation adds a constant fraction of tokens over plain prose, so the runtime must tokenize the exact byte sequence it plans to send.

Wire framing adds further tokens beyond the visible text. Model APIs wrap messages in control tokens that mark roles, turn boundaries, and tool schemas. Counting only the user prompt or tool output misses that wrapper. When the runtime formats the wire payload locally, it must run the model's own tokenizer over the complete formatted sequence; when a remote service applies its own chat template or hidden system wrapper, the runtime must use the provider's token-counting endpoint and admission rules. Because vocabularies and merge tables differ across model families, a token count from one model does not carry over to another.

The same count applies to generated output. A compact tool call uses fewer output tokens than a long prose explanation wrapping the same call, though the exact count depends on how the call is serialized. Shorter schemas cut latency and token spend only when they keep the fields the runtime needs; dropping required arguments, file paths, or error variants to save a few tokens makes downstream execution brittle.

### Output headroom {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-output-headroom}

A prompt that fits inside the context window can still leave too little room for the model to finish its reply, cutting off a tool call mid-argument. To prevent a long prompt from starving the response, the admission check must reserve **output headroom**\index{Output headroom!definition}\index{Context window!output headroom} before sending the call. Let $\SequenceLength$ denote the length of the fully serialized input prompt, $\ContextWindow$ the total **context window**\index{Context window!definition} (the maximum sequence capacity spanning input and output tokens within a single invocation), and $\OutputLimit$ the reserved generation allowance. Where input tokens and generated tokens share a unified context budget, an admission check must enforce:

$$\SequenceLength \le \ContextWindow - \OutputLimit$$ {#eq-vol3-fm-admission}

This inequality guarantees that an incoming prompt cannot fill the context buffer and leave the model no room to answer. Many services also cap input and output lengths separately alongside the shared window, so the runtime must satisfy both the individual caps and the combined bound. Reasoning models add another wrinkle: they emit intermediate reasoning tokens before the visible answer, and those hidden tokens count against $\OutputLimit$ even when the caller never sees them. A three-line visible reply can exhaust a generous output allowance if the model spent hundreds of hidden reasoning tokens first.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How reasoning models spend generated tokens on intermediate work, and how the runtime budgets them, is developed in @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-reasoning-models.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-invocation-token-budget
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ADMISSION HEADROOM FOR AN INSPECTION REQUEST (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-foundation-model-tokenization, token and image budgets.
# │ Goal: Separate input admission from reserved generation capacity.
# │ Show: Remaining input room and the effect of a model-specific image charge.
# │ How: Use hypothetical service counts; subtract reserved output and input
# │      from the combined window, then add the image contribution.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class InvocationTokenBudget:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    window = 8_192  # hypothetical combined context limit, tokens
    output = 1_024  # scenario: reserved generation allowance, tokens
    text_input = 6_000  # scenario: complete serialized text request, tokens
    image_input = 2_048  # scenario: service-reported additional image charge

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    input_ceiling = window - output
    headroom = input_ceiling - text_input
    multimodal_total = text_input + image_input + output
    excess = multimodal_total - window

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(input_ceiling == 7_168, "Unexpected input ceiling")
    check(headroom == 1_168, "Unexpected remaining input headroom")
    check(multimodal_total == 9_072, "Unexpected multimodal total")
    check(excess == 880, "The image must exceed the reserved request budget")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    window_str = fmt_int(window)
    output_str = fmt_int(output)
    text_input_str = fmt_int(text_input)
    image_input_str = fmt_int(image_input)
    input_ceiling_math = fmt_math(rf"\ContextWindow - \OutputLimit = {window:,} - {output:,} = {input_ceiling:,}")
    headroom_math = fmt_math(rf"{input_ceiling:,} - {text_input:,} = {headroom:,}")
    multimodal_math = fmt_math(rf"{text_input:,} + {image_input:,} + {output:,} = {multimodal_total:,}")
    excess_str = fmt_int(excess)
```

Suppose the repair interface has a combined window of `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.window_str` tokens, and the runtime reserves `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.output_str` tokens for generation. Its input ceiling is `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.input_ceiling_math` tokens. If the fully serialized request occupies `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.text_input_str` tokens, `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.headroom_math` tokens of room remain for additional input while preserving the response allowance. The limits are scenario values, not a named model's specification.

If an incoming tool observation exceeds this remaining headroom, the admission check fails. The runtime can then compress prompt history, extract a narrower file slice, or route the call to an execution profile with a larger context window. Shrinking the output allowance $\OutputLimit$ to force admission is risky, as it leaves the model insufficient room to complete complex tool invocations or structured plans. Similarly, silently truncating tool outputs to squeeze them into the remaining margin can strip away the critical stack trace or diagnostic error that the agent needs to resolve the bug.

Even when a request satisfies admission checks, generation can still hit the output token ceiling mid-stream. The runtime must never confuse a syntactically well-formed prefix with a successfully terminated generation. A truncated JSON object may happen to pass a lenient parser if closed artificially, yet it remains an incomplete execution plan. While a partial payload provides valuable diagnostic telemetry, executing it as an intact tool call can cause downstream corruption. The invocation contract in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract turns this boundary into an explicit rule that reads the call's status before its payload.

### Counting multimodal inputs {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-multimodal-accounting}

Attaching a screenshot of a failing dashboard or user-interface (UI) render to a repair request can push a prompt that fit in text well past the context limit. A vision front-end maps each image into a sequence of context positions, and although vision transformers slice images into uniform patches [@dosovitskiy2021image], preprocessing steps such as dynamic tiling, resolution scaling, and spatial pooling mean the billed token count rarely equals a simple patch count.

Consider the earlier budget when adding this visual artifact. If the service reports that the image and its framing tokens require an additional `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.image_input_str` context positions, the total request demand expands to `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.multimodal_math` tokens. This total exceeds the `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.window_str`-token context window by `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.excess_str` tokens, triggering an immediate admission failure before dispatch. The runtime must step in before calling the model. Downscaling the image cuts its token count under some vision backends, but heavy compression can blur single-character error codes or fine trace lines. Budgeting multimodal inputs therefore trades visual detail against the context ceiling.

::: {#chk-02-context-exhaustion-quarantine .callout-checkpoint title="Admitting the next repair request"}

The repair agent is about to add a source excerpt and a diagnostic image to its next call. Its output allowance must remain available for a complete proposal.

- [ ] **Input budget**: Can you identify which message and tool-definition framing must be counted beyond the visible source excerpt?
- [ ] **Output headroom**: With the window fixed at `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.window_str` tokens and the image added, would halving the output reservation make the request fit? Compute the remaining excess, and state what the smaller reservation risks.
- [ ] **Generation status**: If a returned fragment parses successfully after the output limit is reached, can you explain why it is still not a completed candidate?

:::

Token accounting checks upfront that the full request fits with room reserved for the reply. Admission, however, covers only starting capacity. Once decoding begins, token-by-token autoregressive generation determines how that reserved headroom is spent and whether the call finishes cleanly or stops mid-stream.

## Autoregressive Generation {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-autoregressive}

Even when a request fixes the conversation history and the list of available tool schemas, the model's reply remains open-ended and stochastic. On the same repair prompt, one call might propose `read_file` on a configuration path, a second might inspect a different directory, and a third might return prose instead of a tool call. Understanding how the serving engine generates tokens one step at a time explains how to set token budgets and sampling parameters, why repeating a live API call can produce a different trajectory, and why only replaying a recorded response reproduces downstream execution exactly.

### Token-by-token generation {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-conditional-token-selection}

When a model emits a file path inside a `read_file` argument, it chooses each token from learned statistical patterns without checking the filesystem, and that early choice conditions every closing delimiter and reasoning token that follows. Autoregressive language models generate text by factoring the joint probability of a sequence into a product of conditional next-token distributions [@bengio2003neural]. Let $\InputTokenSequence$ denote the input tokens and $\OutputTokenSequence$ an output sequence. Its conditional probability factors as

$$\Pr(\OutputTokenSequence \mid \InputTokenSequence) = \prod_{t=1}^{\OutputLength} \Pr(\OutputToken_t \mid \InputTokenSequence, \OutputTokenPrefix)$$ {#eq-autoregressive-factorization}

At output position $\TokenIndex$, the model with parameters $\ModelParameters$ produces one score, or **logit**\index{Logits!definition}, for each token in vocabulary $\TokenVocabulary$:

$$\LogitVector_t = \NextTokenLogitFunction(\InputTokenSequence, \OutputTokenPrefix) \in \mathbb{R}^{|\TokenVocabulary|}$$

A decoding rule selects a token from these scores and appends it to the prefix for position $\TokenIndex+1$, so early token choices cascade through the rest of the sequence. In an inference serving engine, the decode loop reads the prompt, computes next-token logits, picks an output token, appends it to the prefix, and repeats until a stop condition fires. Generation ends normally when the model emits an end-of-sequence token or matches a caller-supplied stop sequence. It can also stop early at the output token ceiling, or abort on a timeout or network drop. Serving interfaces must report which stop condition fired: an incomplete JSON object cut off at the token limit needs different handling than a finished tool call, and even a clean stop sequence says only that generation ended, not that the task succeeded.

Production Transformer implementations [@vaswani2017] avoid recomputing earlier tokens at every decode step by keeping a *key-value (KV) cache*:[^fn-kv-cache-derived] memory buffers holding the attention keys and values already computed for earlier positions. For a given full-attention architecture and precision, keeping more tokens in flight takes more cache memory. That cache is transient serving state, not an audit log of which tools ran or what they changed. @Sec-vol3-kv-cache covers cache layout and sizing; for a single call, the key point is that both prompt tokens and generated tokens occupy memory during the call.

[^fn-kv-cache-derived]: **Key-Value (KV) Cache**: In causal attention, key and value vectors at a given position depend solely on that token and its predecessors, so once computed they remain static throughout subsequent sequence expansion. Retaining them in device memory turns each new decode step from full-sequence recomputation into a single new row projection per layer alongside a read of stored rows. Consequently, cache capacity and memory bandwidth, rather than floating-point arithmetic, become the primary operational constraints as context windows expand. \index{KV cache!why reuse is exact}

Because each generated token extends a dependent sequence, output length is a major cost variable of a call, and the serving implementation sets its realized latency. Although the conditional dependence in @eq-autoregressive-factorization fixes the mathematical order of token choices, it does not mandate that hardware evaluate each token in an isolated forward pass. Techniques such as speculative decoding,[^fn-speculative-decoding-equivalence] for example, draft candidate token blocks with a small auxiliary model and score them in parallel with the target model, provably preserving the target output distribution [@leviathan2023fast; @chen2023accelerating]. The per-token decode floor derived in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost is therefore a property of plain one-token-per-pass decoding, not a law of the factorization.

[^fn-speculative-decoding-equivalence]: **Speculative Decoding**: The target distribution is preserved by a modified rejection-sampling rule that accepts each drafted token with exactly the probability needed for the accepted sequence to follow the target model's distribution [@leviathan2023fast; @chen2023accelerating]. The guarantee is distributional, not bitwise. Speculative decoding reduces accelerator passes per generated token without changing which candidates can appear, so it leaves the reproducibility questions of @sec-vol3-foundation-model-repetition-replay unchanged. \index{Speculative decoding!distribution preservation}

### Sampling controls {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-sampling-controls}

Lowering sampling randomness can make a model repeat its top-scoring token choice, yet the highest-scoring token is often a plausible guess rather than a valid file path or a working patch. For positive **temperature**\index{Temperature (sampling)!definition}[^fn-sampling-temperature-origin] $\SamplingTemperature$ (subscripted to keep it distinct from the trajectory $\Trajectory$), softmax converts the logits into next-token probabilities:

$$\Pr(\OutputToken_t = \VocabularyToken \mid \InputTokenSequence, \OutputTokenPrefix) = \frac{\exp\left(\OutputLogit_{t, \VocabularyToken} / \SamplingTemperature\right)}{\sum_{\NormalizerTokenIndex \in \TokenVocabulary} \exp\left(\OutputLogit_{t, \NormalizerTokenIndex} / \SamplingTemperature\right)}$$ {#eq-temperature-softmax}

Unit temperature ($\SamplingTemperature = 1.0$) leaves the logits unscaled. Lowering a positive temperature amplifies logit differences and concentrates probability mass on the highest-scoring tokens; raising it flattens the distribution, which approaches uniformity across a finite vocabulary as temperature grows without bound. Temperature therefore controls output entropy, not model confidence: because next-token cross-entropy training minimizes sequence prediction error rather than calibrating scores to task success, high token probability does not mean a completed response is correct.

[^fn-sampling-temperature-origin]: **Temperature**: The term comes from statistical mechanics, where the Boltzmann distribution weights a state of energy $\BoltzmannStateEnergy$ by $\exp(-\BoltzmannStateEnergy/\BoltzmannConstant \BoltzmannTemperature)$; reading each negative logit as an energy makes @eq-temperature-softmax identical in form. In a physical system, high temperature spreads particles across many states, whereas low temperature concentrates them near the ground state. In language model decoding, scaling temperature trades candidate diversity against concentration on the mode without changing which token scores highest. \index{Temperature (sampling)!Boltzmann origin}

**Greedy decoding**\index{Greedy decoding!definition} instead picks a highest-scoring token, $\operatorname{argmax}_{\VocabularyToken \in \TokenVocabulary} \OutputLogit_{t, \VocabularyToken}$, with a tie-breaking rule. Given fixed logits and a fixed tie rule, that choice is deterministic. Serving APIs often expose greedy decoding as $\SamplingTemperature = 0$, which the engine implements by taking the argmax directly rather than dividing by zero in @eq-temperature-softmax. As positive temperature approaches zero, softmax puts all probability mass on the maximum, though if several tokens tie for the top logit, the limit alone does not pick among them.

Sampling can also restrict which tokens remain eligible. **Top-$\TopTokenSampleCount$ sampling**\index{Top-k sampling!definition} [@fan2018hierarchical] keeps the $\TopTokenSampleCount$ highest-scoring tokens under a tie rule and renormalizes their probabilities. **Top-$\NucleusProbabilityMass$ sampling**\index{Top-p sampling!definition}, or nucleus sampling, sorts tokens by descending probability, keeps the shortest prefix whose cumulative mass reaches $\NucleusProbabilityMass$ [@holtzman2020curious], and renormalizes that set. Because top-$\TopTokenSampleCount$ fixes the candidate count regardless of shape, it can keep unlikely tail tokens when the distribution is sharp and cut plausible options when the distribution is flat; top-$\NucleusProbabilityMass$ lets the active pool expand or shrink with the distribution's spread. When temperature scaling and truncation are used together, the order in which they run and the engine's numerical conventions are part of the decoding configuration.

Neither filter tells valid file paths, true claims, or safe commands from wrong ones. A rare token may be the exact identifier a patch needs, while a high-probability continuation may name a file that does not exist. Truncation filters change which candidates reach the runtime; only checks against the environment and task contract tell whether that change helps.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/nucleus_truncation_margin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Five probability bars for tokens v1 to v5 at unit temperature. v1 is labeled 78 percent and v2 17 percent, both in blue under a bracket labeled top-p 0.90. v3 is a short gray bar at about 4 percent and v4 and v5 are gray hairlines, together marked by the label tail cut, which top-p discards before renormalizing."}

*Nucleus truncation keeps the two tokens whose mass reaches 0.90 and zeroes the gray tail.*
:::

```{python}
#| label: lego-logit-scaling-truncation
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LOGIT SCALING AND TRUNCATION (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-02-logit-scaling-and-truncation-on
# │ Goal: Compare temperature and nucleus sampling for the same hypothetical logits.
# │ Show: Sharpening and truncation redistribute probability, not correctness.
# │ How: Normalize exponentials, select a cumulative-probability prefix, renormalize.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_math, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent

class LogitScalingTruncation:
    """Sampling transformations for a fixed hypothetical vocabulary."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    logits = [12.0, 10.5, 9.0, 6.0, 3.0]
    tau_base = 1.0
    tau_sharp = 0.5
    p_nucleus = 0.90

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    exp_tau1 = []
    for z in logits:
        exp_tau1.append(math.exp(z / tau_base))
    sum_exp_tau1 = sum(exp_tau1)
    probs_tau1 = []
    for e in exp_tau1:
        probs_tau1.append(e / sum_exp_tau1)
    exp_tau05 = []
    for z in logits:
        exp_tau05.append(math.exp(z / tau_sharp))
    sum_exp_tau05 = sum(exp_tau05)
    probs_tau05 = []
    for e in exp_tau05:
        probs_tau05.append(e / sum_exp_tau05)
    sum_nuc = probs_tau1[0] + probs_tau1[1]
    p_nuc_v1 = probs_tau1[0] / sum_nuc
    p_nuc_v2 = probs_tau1[1] / sum_nuc
    tail_base = 1 - probs_tau1[0]  # probability of drawing any non-top token
    tail_sharp = 1 - probs_tau05[0]
    tail_ratio = tail_base / tail_sharp

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(sum(probs_tau1) - 1.0) < 1e-12, "Baseline distribution must normalize")
    check(abs(sum(probs_tau05) - 1.0) < 1e-12, "Sharpened distribution must normalize")
    check(abs(probs_tau1[0] - 0.7840) < 0.001, "Unexpected tau=1.0 top prob")
    check(abs(probs_tau05[0] - 0.950324648968) < 1e-9, "Unexpected tau=0.5 top prob")
    check(abs(sum_nuc - 0.9589) < 0.001, "Unexpected nucleus denominator")
    check(probs_tau1[0] < p_nucleus <= sum_nuc, "Nucleus must contain exactly two tokens")
    check(abs(p_nuc_v1 - 0.8176) < 0.001, "Unexpected nucleus v1 prob")
    check(abs(p_nuc_v2 - 0.1824) < 0.001, "Unexpected nucleus v2 prob")
    check(abs(p_nuc_v1 + p_nuc_v2 - 1.0) < 1e-12, "Nucleus must normalize")
    check(3 < tail_ratio < 6, "Halving temperature should shrink the non-top tail several-fold")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    logits_math = fmt_math(rf"\LogitVector_t = [{', '.join(f'{v:g}' for v in logits)}]")
    base_vector_math = fmt_math(rf"\UnitTemperatureProbabilityVector \approx [{', '.join(f'{v:.4f}' for v in probs_tau1)}]")
    sharp_first_str = fmt(probs_tau05[0], precision=4, commas=False)
    sum_exp_tau1_str = fmt(sum_exp_tau1, precision=1, commas=False)
    tau_base_str = fmt(tau_base, precision=0, commas=False)
    tau_sharp_str = fmt(tau_sharp, precision=1, commas=False)
    top_mass_pct_str = fmt_percent(probs_tau05[0], precision=1, style="prose")
    p_nucleus_str = fmt(p_nucleus, precision=2, commas=False)
    first_prob_str = fmt(probs_tau1[0], precision=4, commas=False)
    second_prob_str = fmt(probs_tau1[1], precision=4, commas=False)
    nucleus_mass_str = fmt(sum_nuc, precision=4, commas=False)
    nucleus_first_str = fmt(p_nuc_v1, precision=4, commas=False)
    nucleus_second_str = fmt(p_nuc_v2, precision=4, commas=False)
    tail_base_pct_str = fmt_percent(tail_base, precision=1, style="prose")
    tail_sharp_pct_str = fmt_percent(tail_sharp, precision=1, style="prose")
    tail_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(tail_ratio, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-02-logit-scaling-and-truncation-on .callout-notebook title="Temperature and truncation on the same logits"}

**Problem**: A hypothetical vocabulary $\TokenVocabulary = \{\VocabularyToken_1, \VocabularyToken_2, \VocabularyToken_3, \VocabularyToken_4, \VocabularyToken_5\}$ has logits `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.logits_math`, held fixed so that differences arise strictly from the decoding configuration. How much probability mass concentrates onto the top token when halving the temperature, and which tokens survive nucleus truncation?

**Math**: At temperature $\SamplingTemperature =$ `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.tau_base_str`, the exponentiated logits sum to `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.sum_exp_tau1_str`. Normalizing each exponential by this partition sum yields the baseline distribution:

`{python} LogitScalingTruncation.base_vector_math`.

Halving the temperature to $\SamplingTemperature =$ `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.tau_sharp_str` doubles the exponent of each term. Following normalization, the probability of the mode $\VocabularyToken_1$ rises to `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.sharp_first_str`, capturing `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.top_mass_pct_str` of the total distribution. All lower-ranked tokens retain positive probability under untruncated softmax.

Returning to unit temperature and applying nucleus truncation with $\NucleusProbabilityMass =$ `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.p_nucleus_str` evaluates cumulative probability mass. The lead token $\VocabularyToken_1$ provides `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.first_prob_str`, which falls short of the threshold. Incorporating $\VocabularyToken_2$ (`{python} LogitScalingTruncation.second_prob_str`) brings cumulative coverage to `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.nucleus_mass_str`, which satisfies the threshold and defines the active nucleus as $\{\VocabularyToken_1, \VocabularyToken_2\}$. Renormalizing across this active set assigns probability `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.nucleus_first_str` to $\VocabularyToken_1$ and `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.nucleus_second_str` to $\VocabularyToken_2$, while strictly zeroing the remaining tail tokens $\{\VocabularyToken_3, \VocabularyToken_4, \VocabularyToken_5\}$.

**Systems insight**: Temperature governs candidate diversity. Halving temperature compresses the non-top probability tail from `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.tail_base_pct_str` to `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.tail_sharp_pct_str`, achieving a `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.tail_ratio_mult_str` reduction, whereas nucleus truncation eliminates the tail entirely. Repeated calls produce diverse outputs only when probability mass occupies this tail, which is the stochastic resource that parallel candidate sampling draws on in @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-breadth-axis. Because neither transformation ensures that the highest-scoring candidate is correct, engineering teams configure decoding parameters based on empirical task pass rates rather than raw model likelihood.

:::

### Repetition and replay {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-repetition-replay}

Greedy decoding removes sampling variance from a fixed logit vector, but it does not make served API calls reproducible end to end. In a production cluster, two identical requests can land on different server nodes, accelerator revisions, or kernel builds. Small differences in floating-point reduction order[^fn-float-reduction-order] can shift nearly tied logits in their least significant bits, and flipping an argmax choice at position $\TokenIndex=1$ changes the prefix for every token after it. Fixing a pseudorandom seed controls the sampler's random number generator, but it cannot prevent numerical differences across backend kernels or dynamic batch sizes. Reproducing a call from scratch requires pinning the serving environment and kernels as well as setting $\SamplingTemperature = 0$. A 2025 production incident shows how serving-fleet bugs alone can change model outputs while caller requests stay identical.

[^fn-float-reduction-order]: **Floating-Point Reduction Order**: Floating-point addition is not associative because each intermediate sum rounds [@goldberg1991]. Parallel attention and reduction kernels that sum dot products across different thread-block layouts or dynamic batch sizes add numbers in different orders, so the same request can produce logits that differ in their low bits depending on which other requests share its batch. \index{Floating-point arithmetic!nondeterministic reduction}

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-fm-serving-postmortem
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SERVING-PATH INCIDENT FIGURES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: ws-02-anthropic-serving-bugs-2025 and the replay fallacy in
# │          @sec-vol3-foundation-model-fallacies.
# │ Goal: Carry the incident's reported shares as named, sourced inputs.
# │ Show: Worst-hour share of one model's requests misrouted; share of one
# │       tool's users with at least one misrouted message.
# │ How: Values as reported in anthropic2025postmortem; no computation.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_percent

class ServingPostmortem:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    worst_hour_share = 0.16  # sourced: anthropic2025postmortem, worst hour, one model's requests misrouted
    user_share = 0.30  # sourced: anthropic2025postmortem, approx. share of coding-tool users affected

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Reported values only.

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < worst_hour_share < user_share < 1, "Reported shares must be fractions in source order")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    worst_hour_pct_str = fmt_percent(worst_hour_share, precision=0, style="prose")
    user_pct_str = fmt_percent(user_share, precision=0, style="prose")
```

::: {#ws-02-anthropic-serving-bugs-2025 .callout-war-story title="Three serving bugs behind unchanged requests (2025)"}

**Context**: Between August and early September 2025, three separate infrastructure bugs intermittently degraded the responses of Anthropic's Claude models [@anthropic2025postmortem]. These defects stemmed entirely from the serving infrastructure rather than caller requests or model weights.

**Mechanism**: A front-end routing defect directed standard traffic to server clusters configured for extended context windows, while session stickiness (routing a client's follow-up requests to the server that handled its earlier ones) kept those follow-up requests on the misconfigured nodes. Concurrently, an improperly deployed kernel optimization on a specialized accelerator cluster occasionally assigned outsized probability to improbable tokens. Finally, an optimization in the token-selection pipeline triggered a compiler bug: an approximate top-$\TopTokenSampleCount$ routine with mixed-precision subroutines emitted incorrect tokens under specific dynamic batch sizes.

**Impact**: During peak impact, the routing failure corrupted `{python} ServingPostmortem.worst_hour_pct_str` of requests to one production model, and approximately `{python} ServingPostmortem.user_pct_str` of active coding agent users encountered at least one misrouted interaction. Generated responses contained foreign-language script insertions within English prose and syntax anomalies in generated source code. Automated regression suites initially missed these failures because a response often recovered from an isolated corrupted token later in generation, and intermittent runtime conditions meant an identical prompt could succeed on one invocation and fail on the next.

**Fix**: Engineers rolled back the offending kernel deployments, corrected cluster routing rules, and replaced the approximate top-$\TopTokenSampleCount$ kernel with an exact selection routine running in 32-bit floating-point precision, trading a minor throughput penalty for numerical stability. Anthropic subsequently deployed continuous canary evaluations across production fleets to catch subtle generational drift.

**Systems lesson**: Output distributions reflect the concrete serving pipeline just as heavily as the model weights or input context. Corrupted tokens arrived packaged in well-formed HTTP payloads and cleanly closed generation blocks, a direct instance of the fail-plausible fault (@sec-vol3-intro-fail-plausible). Agent runtimes must log full call-level metadata (runtime versions, routing tags, and sampling parameters) while subjecting every proposed action to external environment validation regardless of nominal generation success.

:::

Incidents like this one set the logging baseline for an agent runtime. The runtime log should record the serialized prompt, model and tokenizer identifiers, sampling settings, token limits, and any routing or seed metadata, alongside the raw response payload, stop reason, and token usage. Those records also separate two kinds of debugging: replaying a recorded response tests the runtime's downstream logic without model variance, whereas re-sending the live request tests how the agent handles variation across calls. Benchmarks should measure and report that call-to-call variance rather than judging a configuration from a single run.

An agent runtime therefore receives candidate tokens produced under a specific decoding configuration and ended by a specific stop condition. That stop condition is the first thing the runtime must read. A generation that ran into its output ceiling, was refused, or was cut off in transit can still deliver bytes that look like a finished proposal, and no check on the payload alone tells the difference. Before asking whether a `read_file` proposal names an existing, permitted path, the runtime needs a record of whether a complete candidate arrived at all.

## The Invocation Contract {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract}

Suppose a model begins generating a cleanup command targeting the path `/tmp/scratch/cache_dir`, but reaches its token limit immediately after emitting `/tmp/scratch`. Both strings form syntactically valid shell commands, yet they specify different deletion boundaries. An execution engine inspecting only raw text cannot determine whether the shorter path represents an intended command or a truncated prefix. To prevent an unintended deletion, the host runtime requires an explicit execution outcome alongside the payload, pairing each request specification with a normalized response envelope at the invocation boundary so that every remote generation is governed by a unified contract.

::: {#dfn-vol3-model-invocation-contract .callout-definition title="Model invocation contract"}

***Model invocation contract***\index{Model invocation contract!definition} is the pair of records that bounds one model call: a request fixing the input, model configuration, sampling settings, and enforced output and time limits, and a normalized envelope reporting the call's status, payload, and resource use.

1.  **Significance**: The contract establishes each model call as a distinct, countable unit within an agent trajectory. Its usage record prices the call's share of $\AttemptCost$, and its status flag isolates completed generations from partial or failed calls. Consequently, the cost per accepted task (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task) can be computed from recorded telemetry rather than heuristically reconstructed from conversation transcripts.
2.  **Distinction**: The invocation contract describes the model call rather than the overarching task. A generated tool request can fully conform to decoding limits without ever being dispatched, and a fully generated response can fail downstream validation. Dispatch authorization, tool execution, and task-level acceptance remain separate runtime decisions backed by their own evidence.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Recording only the payload text. Without explicit status flags and usage accounting, a truncated fragment is indistinguishable from an intentional short response, and unrecorded token consumption silently distorts operational cost accounting as zero-cost execution.

:::

### What a request specifies {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-request-specification}

Leaving any part of a model request implicit—an unpinned model alias that silently updates, an unenforced token cap, or an unrecorded sampling setting—makes it impossible to price the call or explain why its behavior changed. At the generation interface, the bounded request fixes six fields:

$$\ModelCallRequest = \langle \RequestPromptTokens, \text{ModelID}, \OutputLimit, \CompletionDeadline, \StopSequenceSet, \SamplingParameters \rangle$$

The first field, $\RequestPromptTokens = (\PromptToken_1, \PromptToken_2, \dots, \PromptToken_{\SequenceLength})$, encodes the serialized messages, role markers, advertised tool schemas, and formatting delimiters visible to the model, which the runtime builds from structured `messages` and `tools` inputs before serialization. Once the input sequence is fixed, `ModelID` and $\SamplingParameters$ specify how the serving stack evaluates it. `ModelID` names the model weights and serving deployment selected through `model_config`, where engineers distinguish mutable provider aliases (such as `model-latest`) from pinned, immutable revisions (such as dated or content-addressed snapshots). The sampling parameters $\SamplingParameters$, including temperature and top-$\NucleusProbabilityMass$, then fix the selection rule used during decoding. Together with the serialized input and returned output, those fields document the call; exact regeneration also depends on the serving path, as war story \ref{ws-02-anthropic-serving-bugs-2025} showed.

To bound how long that generation may run, the request pairs an output allowance $\OutputLimit$ with a local waiting deadline $\CompletionDeadline$. Because a system cannot rely on the model to stop on time, invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}) places both limits below the model, where the host runtime and serving system enforce them mechanically. Before sending the call, the runtime checks that the prompt and output allowance fit inside the context window, and the adapter notes whether the provider bills hidden reasoning tokens against $\OutputLimit$, since counting only visible text would understate what the call spent.

Generation can also end before reaching $\OutputLimit$ when the output matches one of the stop sequences in $\StopSequenceSet$, which halt decoding as soon as the serving engine encounters them. Because the engine matches raw byte or character sequences without parsing structure, a stop sequence that appears inside an argument or quoted string can cut off generation before the closing quotes or braces are emitted. The runtime must therefore record the provider's stop reason and validate syntax separately.

Resource limits are enforced in two places: on the client host and on the remote serving cluster. Locally, the host runtime caps incoming response bytes and stops waiting when the deadline $\CompletionDeadline$ expires. A local timeout ends the caller's wait and marks the call failed, but it does not prove that the remote server stopped decoding or freed accelerator memory.[^fn-rpc-unknown-outcome] Server-side token caps and cancellation protocols handle the remote side, so every limit should state which component enforces it and which resource it bounds.

[^fn-rpc-unknown-outcome]: **Remote Call Semantics**: Remote procedure call designers met this ambiguity first. In the design @birrell1984rpc describe, a call that returns normally executed exactly once, but a call that ends in a failure report may have executed once or not at all, because the caller cannot tell a lost request from a lost reply. A model call inherits the same gap: a timed-out generation may still have run to completion and been billed, which is why the normalized status for a failed delivery, `TRANSPORT_FAILURE` (@tbl-vol3-invocation-status), records an unknown remote outcome rather than a call that never happened. \index{Remote procedure call!unknown outcome}

### The normalized status envelope {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-status-envelope}

If a runtime inspects only the returned text or tool arguments, a partial string cut off by a token ceiling looks just like a finished proposal. To keep how a call ended attached to what it returned, the runtime wraps every response in a **normalized status envelope**\index{Normalized status envelope!definition}:

$$\NormalizedStatusEnvelope = \langle \text{status}, \ResponsePayload, \ResponseMetadata \rangle$$

Here, $\ResponsePayload$ is the returned payload, which may be complete, partial, or empty, and $\ResponseMetadata$ holds the call's telemetry: the response `kind`, the raw provider `stop_reason`, reported token `usage`, request identifiers, latency timestamps, and serving settings. Keeping $\ResponsePayload$ paired with $\ResponseMetadata$ prevents downstream code from reading the payload without its status, and records unreported usage as unknown rather than zero.

Because different model APIs report stop reasons, error codes, and transport failures in incompatible ways, the runtime adapter maps provider-specific signals onto the seven normalized statuses in @tbl-vol3-invocation-status. Two of them, `REJECTED` and `CANCELED`, occur only while a response is streaming (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-streaming-cancellation). Each status records what the host runtime verified locally; if two events race, such as a local cancellation crossing an incoming completion frame, the adapter resolves the status deterministically while keeping the raw provider signals in $\ResponseMetadata$.

| Status flag         | Terminal condition                                                               | Payload integrity                                                              | Admissible host action                                               |
|:--------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `COMPLETED`         | Confirmed normal generation termination within the call's limits                 | Fully generated according to the protocol; syntax and meaning remain unchecked | Admit to candidate validation, not directly to dispatch              |
| `TRUNCATED`         | Generation reaches a token or context ceiling before confirmed normal completion | Incomplete candidate that may nevertheless parse                               | Withhold from action; record the limit and diagnose                  |
| `REFUSED`           | The model or service explicitly declines the request or response                 | Refusal notice, partial content, or no payload                                 | Handle under the task's refusal policy; do not treat as an action    |
| `TRANSPORT_FAILURE` | Delivery fails or the local deadline expires without accepted completion         | Missing or partial content; remote outcome may be unknown                      | Record uncertainty and apply bounded failure handling                |
| `REJECTED`          | A runtime monitor rejects the response during reception                          | Content observed before rejection                                              | Withhold from action; record the rejection and request cancellation  |
| `CANCELED`          | Discretionary runtime or operator cancellation before accepted completion        | Partial, missing, or otherwise unusable as a completed candidate               | Stop local candidate processing; track remote termination separately |
| `FAULTED`           | The service reports an execution failure                                         | Missing, partial, or diagnostic content                                        | Record the reported fault and route to failure handling              |
: **Normalized invocation status envelope**: Status controls admission to the candidate path. Completion is a generation outcome, while authorization, tool execution, and task acceptance remain separate decisions. {#tbl-vol3-invocation-status tbl-colwidths="[21,27,25,27]"}

For a `read_file` request, `kind="tool_request"` tells the runtime which schema to check, while `status="COMPLETED"` confirms that generation finished normally. Neither field says that the tool ran or that the file read succeeded; completion describes generation, whereas tool execution and task acceptance are separate runtime decisions.

Applying invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}) to the status field gives a hard gate: the **quarantining rule**\index{Quarantining rule!definition}. Under this rule, no payload whose status is anything other than `COMPLETED` may enter the candidate validation or tool-dispatch path. The runtime checks `status` before parsing or dispatching the payload. It can log an interrupted or malformed fragment for diagnosis, but that log entry cannot trigger a tool call or be promoted to a finished proposal. When later chapters sample several candidates for one task, any candidate cut off by a token limit obeys the same rule: a truncated payload is a diagnosable failure, never a partial action.

The cleanup command introduced earlier shows why parsing alone cannot replace this status check. Suppose the complete intended command is

```bash
rm -rf /tmp/scratch/cache_dir
```

If an exhausted token quota cuts off generation mid-path, the prefix is

```bash
rm -rf /tmp/scratch
```

That truncated prefix is valid shell syntax, yet it deletes the entire parent directory. Because the envelope marks the call `TRUNCATED`, the quarantining rule blocks the command before it reaches the shell. Conversely, `status="COMPLETED"` grants no permission to run; it establishes only that the model finished emitting its proposal. @Lst-vol3-completed-candidate-gate implements this admission check, passing only completed generations to the candidate path while leaving syntax, permissions, and task verification to later stages.

::: {#lst-vol3-completed-candidate-gate lst-cap="**Completed-candidate admission**: The status check admits only completed generations to the candidate path. Returning the payload grants no execution authority."}
```python
def completed_candidate(envelope):
    if envelope["status"] != "COMPLETED":
        raise ValueError("Response is not a completed candidate")
    # Syntax, permission, and task evidence remain unchecked.
    return envelope["payload"]
```
:::

Incomplete payloads go to a diagnostic log with its own storage and access limits, keeping the partial byte stream and `stop_reason` for debugging. "Repairing" a truncated fragment by appending guessed arguments or closing braces invents a new candidate that the model never completed, and such patched fragments must never be marked `COMPLETED`.

### Streaming and cancellation {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-streaming-cancellation}

Waiting for a four-thousand-token response to finish before checking its structure wastes seconds of accelerator time when the first key violates the tool schema. **Streaming**\index{Streaming!definition} delivers response fragments over the connection as generation proceeds, letting the runtime inspect prefixes early—provided its parser follows the provider's framing protocol rather than assuming each network chunk holds one token. When an arriving prefix violates the required format, the stream monitor stops waiting immediately instead of buffering the rest of an unusable reply. Because generation is still in flight, the monitor checks whether the prefix can still be completed into a valid structure, not whether it is already complete.

Rejection and cancellation are distinct events. When the stream monitor spots a structural violation, the runtime sets the status to `REJECTED` and sends a cancel request to the service. When an operator or runtime policy aborts a compliant stream before completion, the runtime marks the status `CANCELED`. A local deadline that expires before completion maps instead to `TRANSPORT_FAILURE` (@tbl-vol3-invocation-status), after which the runtime may also send a cancel request. Keeping the partial payload out of tool dispatch is a local guarantee the host enforces in all three cases. Stopping the remote decode loop and freeing accelerator memory, however, depends on the serving engine honoring the cancel signal; merely closing a client socket does not prove that remote decoding stopped.

```{python}
#| label: lego-stream-cancel
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ GENERATION WORK SPARED BY EARLY CANCELLATION (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract, streaming and cancellation;
# │          @fig-vol3-streaming-cancellation.
# │ Goal: Bound the decode work a honored cancel request can avoid.
# │ Show: 4,000 skipped decode steps; their time at the reference output floor.
# │ How: (K_max - t_cut) steps times the weight-transfer floor per output token,
# │      the same floor that CallPrice uses in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_INT8, param
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_count, fmt_time

class StreamCancel:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    accel = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    weight_bytes = BYTES_INT8
    k_cap = 4_096  # scenario: output allowance of the canceled call (as drawn in the figure)
    k_cut = 96  # scenario: decode step at which the stream monitor rejects (as drawn)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_dec = ((model.parameters / param * weight_bytes) / accel.memory.bandwidth).to(second)
    cancel_steps = k_cap - k_cut
    cancel_s = cancel_steps * t_dec

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(cancel_steps == 4_000, "The figure labels 4,000 decode steps not run")
    check(cancel_s > 10 * second, "Early cancellation should spare tens of seconds of decode")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    k_cap_str = fmt_count(k_cap)
    k_cut_str = fmt_count(k_cut)
    cancel_steps_str = fmt_count(cancel_steps)
    t_dec_ms_str = fmt_time(t_dec, unit=ms, precision=3)
    cancel_s_str = fmt_time(cancel_s, unit=second, precision=1)
```

Consider a call with an output allowance of `{python} StreamCancel.k_cap_str` tokens whose stream validator detects a schema violation at step $\RejectionDecodeStep =$ `{python} StreamCancel.k_cut_str`. The runtime's part of the response finishes at once. It records the rejection, discards the partial proposal, and sends a cancel request. The service's part depends on whether that request is honored (@fig-vol3-streaming-cancellation).

::: {#fig-vol3-streaming-cancellation data-explore="mechanism-scene" data-explore-key="vol3:fig-vol3-streaming-cancellation" fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Reject, Then Cancel**: The runtime's stream validator advances a parser state as each prefix arrives and holds the output rather than acting on it. At step `{python} StreamCancel.k_cut_str` the proposal introduces a key outside the schema, so the runtime records a rejection, discards the partial proposal, and sends a cancel request. The runtime outcomes on the left hold regardless of the service; the service outcomes on the right hold only if the service receives and honors the cancel request." fig-alt="Three lanes. Top, model service: an output allowance bar drawn to scale for 4,096 steps, with a thin solid sliver for the first 96 steps and a long dashed region labeled up to 4,000 decode steps not run. Middle, token stream: a zoom into the sliver shows step 1, an opening brace, step 2, a query key, steps 3 to 95 elided, and step 96, a force key outlined in red. Bottom, agent runtime stream validator: parser transitions q0 to q1 and q1 to q2, each held, and at step 96 a red box marked REJECTED, key not in schema. A red cancel request arrow runs from the rejection up to the dashed region of the allowance bar. Below, runtime outcomes: partial proposal never dispatched, rejection recorded in the envelope, error returned to the model next turn. Service outcomes, if honored: decoding stops at step 96, request leaves the batch, KV cache memory released."}
![](images/svg/streaming_token_cancellation.svg)
:::

The skipped-step count shown is an upper bound that requires provider cooperation. If the serving engine processes the cancellation promptly, it skips up to $\OutputLimit - \RejectionDecodeStep =$ `{python} StreamCancel.cancel_steps_str` autoregressive decode steps. In the reference unbatched deployment, each plain autoregressive decode step reads the model weights from accelerator memory, so the step takes at least the weight bytes divided by the memory bandwidth; for the reference deployment of @sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost, that floor is `{python} StreamCancel.t_dec_ms_str` per generated token. At that reference floor, skipping all these steps avoids `{python} StreamCancel.cancel_s_str` of estimated decode work. An honored cancellation also frees the request's slot among the requests the serving engine decodes together and releases the call's KV-cache allocations. If the remote service fails to honor the cancellation, the host runtime still quarantines the rejected payload locally, but the remote service may continue generating up to its token allowance.

Nonstreaming calls apply the same status gate once the whole response arrives. Streaming moves the check earlier in the call so the runtime can reject bad prefixes and reclaim resources sooner, without relaxing the rule that incomplete prefixes never run. Either way, the status gate settles only whether a complete candidate arrived. A `COMPLETED` `read_file` proposal can still name a missing file or a path outside the workspace, so the next question is what each subsequent check on that candidate actually proves.

## Checking Candidate Outputs {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-continuations}

Suppose the status gate has admitted a completed `read_file` proposal with `path` set to `src/pool.py`. Completion says only that generation finished, and, as the validation and authorization stages in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-proposals-observations showed, schema conformance says nothing about whether the file exists or lies inside the workspace. Generative inference produces a candidate token sequence; neither high statistical likelihood nor schema conformance determines whether the runtime environment can safely act on it.

The same distinction applies when the model emits a source code patch rather than an inspection request. A candidate patch can parse cleanly, compile against existing headers, and pass a sequential unit test while leaving the underlying race condition untouched. Each verification check answers a narrow, specific question rather than certifying overall task satisfaction.
